common_name: De Soto Plum (Historic Iowa Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or grafted stock in late winter to early spring while still dormant, in well-drained soil in full sun; De Soto sets fruit best with a second American plum or compatible hybrid plum nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and site a second seedling or cultivar of American plum nearby, since De Soto is not reliably self-fruitful. Selected from a wild seedling near Lansing, Iowa and distributed by nurseryman Elisha Hale beginning in 1864, De Soto became one of the most widely planted named selections of native American plum during the 19th-century prairie plum boom, prized enough that it was carried on the American Pomological Society's recommended fruit list on and off for decades. It bears clusters of red to reddish-orange, thick-skinned, clingstone fruit with a rich, tangy-sweet flavor that many growers still rate above the wild species for jams, jellies, and preserves. The tree suckers readily to form a small thicket if left unpruned, so remove root sprouts to maintain a single-trunk form, and expect it to shrug off drought, cold, and poor soil once established far better than any modern hybrid plum.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container-grown tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ennis is a female selection valued for setting a heavy crop of seedless fruit, an unusual trait among American persimmon cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and give the tree room to develop its taproot undisturbed, since American persimmon resents transplanting once established. Ennis is one of only a handful of known tetraploid selections of native persimmon, distinguished from the more common hexaploid cultivars by its ability to reliably produce seedless, orange fruit roughly 1-2 inches across. Because of its genetics, Ennis has also been used as breeding stock in programs working toward seedless persimmon cultivars. Let the fruit soften fully on the tree or after a light frost before eating, as unripe fruit is intensely astringent, and expect this tough native tree to tolerate heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care once it is established.
sources: Kentucky State University Persimmon Research Program

common_name: Early Jewel Persimmon (H-118 Claypool Early-Ripening Selection)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container-grown tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Early Jewel ripens earlier than most American persimmon cultivars and bears heavily and annually even as a young tree.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and prune annually if you want to keep the naturally vigorous tree contained to 20-25 feet rather than letting it grow to full native persimmon height. Also sold under its original breeding designation H-118, Early Jewel came out of the late James Claypool's Indiana persimmon breeding program and stands out for ripening its large, reddish-orange fruit in early September, weeks ahead of standard cultivars like Early Golden and Prok, which stretches the harvest season for home growers. The soft, fully ripe fruit carries a distinctive rich butterscotch-and-rum flavor that fans of native persimmon prize highly. It is a strong, reliable annual bearer that comes into production at a relatively young age for the species, and like all American persimmon needs full sun and deep soil to perform its best.
sources: Kentucky State University Persimmon Research Program

common_name: KSU-Chappell Pawpaw (Kentucky State University Large-Fruited Selection)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young; KSU-Chappell needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, siting the tree in partial shade for its first few years before it can handle more sun as it matures. Released in 2018 by Kentucky State University's pawpaw breeding program, following the earlier KSU-Atwood and KSU-Benson introductions, KSU-Chappell is an extremely vigorous, high-yielding cultivar that in multi-year trials averaged notably larger fruit than the widely grown Susquehanna while carrying a comparably low percentage of seed by weight. The creamy flesh has a mild banana-pineapple flavor with floral notes that ripens mid-season, typically September into October. Like all pawpaws, it is self-incompatible and pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so plant a second, unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small brush to improve fruit set in a home orchard.
sources: Kentucky State University Land-Grant Program — Pawpaw Research
American Society for Horticultural Science conference proceedings

common_name: Chico Jujube (USDA Chico Station Fresh-Eating Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Chico has a low chilling requirement of around 200 hours, which suits it well to mild Gulf South winters, and sets a heavier crop with a Li or Lang jujube planted nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and neglect far better than most fruit trees once it is established, which suits the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season well. Chico originated at the USDA's Chico Plant Introduction Station in California as an open-pollinated seedling of the older 'So' (Contorted) jujube, and was released for its medium-to-large, flattened round fruit with a fine, crisp texture. Unlike many jujube cultivars that taste purely sweet, Chico carries a noticeable tang alongside its sweetness, giving it a more balanced flavor that many fresh-eating fans prefer. It is partly self-fruitful, ripens over a long midseason harvest window, and needs only routine pruning to remove root suckers and keep its naturally upright, thorny growth in bounds.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Chico Plant Introduction Station
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension — Jujube

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Shanxi Li is self-fruitful and tolerates extreme summer heat and winter cold once established, making it a low-maintenance choice across a wide range of climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Shanxi Li shrugs off drought, poor soil, and the humid heat of a Gulf South summer far better than most fruit trees, and is naturally resistant to most pests and diseases that trouble other orchard crops. Named for its native Shanxi province in northern China, this heirloom selection produces the largest fruit of the Li-type jujubes, with shiny reddish-brown, date-shaped fruit that can reach over 2 inches long. The crisp, sweet flesh is excellent eaten fresh off the tree and turns into a chewy, date-like treat when dried. Self-fruitful, it will set a good crop on its own, though yields improve with a second jujube cultivar nearby, and the tree handles winter temperatures well below zero once dormant.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension — Jujube
